blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Delhi Sultanate was ruled by five distinct dynasties: Slave (Mamluk), Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, and Lodi from 1206 to 1526 AD.
Iltutmish consolidated the Sultanate, introduced the Iqta system, organized 'Turkan-i-Chahalgani', and issued Silver Tanka and Copper Jital coins.
Alauddin Khalji implemented strict market control policies, fixed prices of commodities, and introduced branding of horses (Dagh) and descriptive rolls of soldiers (Chehra).
Muhammad bin Tughlaq was known for ambitious yet controversial policies like transferring the capital to Daulatabad and issuing token currency.
The Sultanate era concluded in 1526 AD when Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi in the First Battle of Panipat, establishing the Mughal Empire.

blocks.content: The Delhi Sultanate marks the beginning of Muslim rule in India on a large and organized scale. It represents a major turning point in Indian history as it introduced new administrative systems, military organization, land revenue practices, art, architecture, and socio-cultural changes. The Delhi Sultanate existed from 1206 AD to 1526 AD and was ruled by five different dynasties. This period forms the backbone of Medieval Indian History for  examinations.

Qutbuddin Aibak was the founder of the Slave Dynasty and the first Sultan of Delhi. He was a former slave of Muhammad Ghori and became independent after Ghori’s death. He established Turkish rule in India.
Achievements
He constructed the Qutb Minar (completed by Iltutmish) and the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque. He was known as 'Lakh Baksh' for his generosity.
Iltutmish was the real consolidator of the Delhi Sultanate. He organized the administrative machinery and secured the Sultanate from external threats.
Key Reforms
He introduced the Iqta system, established the Chahalgani (group of forty nobles), and issued silver tanka and copper jital coins.
Razia Sultana was the first and only woman ruler of the Delhi Sultanate. She was a capable ruler but faced opposition from the Turkish nobles.
Balban strengthened the Sultanate by enforcing strict discipline. He introduced the policy of 'Blood and Iron'.
Important Concepts under Slave Dynasty
Theory of Kingship, Sijda and Paibos, spy system, strong army, suppression of Turkish nobles.
The Delhi Sultanate established Islamic rule across major parts of the Indian subcontinent from 1206 to 1526 AD.
Alauddin Khilji was the most powerful ruler of the Delhi Sultanate. He expanded the Sultanate to South India and introduced revolutionary reforms.
Alauddin introduced a strict market control system to maintain a large army at low cost. Prices of essential commodities were fixed.
He introduced branding of horses (Dagh) and descriptive rolls (Chehra).
He introduced measurement of land and fixed land revenue at 50% of produce.

rows: Qutb-ud-din Aibak, Iltutmish, Razia Sultan, Balban
Consolidation of Delhi Sultanate, Iqta system, creation of Chahalgani, theory of divine kingship.
Southern imperial expansion, strict price and market control mechanisms, introduction of Dagh and Chehra.
Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, Muhammad bin Tughlaq, Firoz Shah Tughlaq
Capital transfer attempt, token currency experiment, extensive canal irrigation system, creation of public works departments.
Established post-Timur invasion; relatively short-lived rule with limited administrative territorial control.
Bahlul Lodi, Sikandar Lodi, Ibrahim Lodi
First Afghan dynasty of Delhi, founding of Agra (1504), ended with the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.

blocks.content: Muhammad bin Tughlaq was the most controversial ruler of the Delhi Sultanate. He was highly intelligent but his policies failed due to poor implementation.
Major Experiments
Transfer of capital to Daulatabad, token currency, heavy taxation in Doab, Khurasan expedition.
Firoz Shah Tughlaq followed a policy of benevolence. He established public works, canals, hospitals, and madrasas.
The Sayyids ruled as deputies of Timur. They had very weak authority and limited territorial control.
Bahlol Lodi founded the Lodi dynasty and was the first Afghan ruler of Delhi.
Sikandar Lodi was an efficient administrator and patron of learning.
Ibrahim Lodi was an unpopular ruler whose defeat by Babur in 1526 AD ended the Delhi Sultanate.
The administration of the Delhi Sultanate was highly centralized. The Sultan was the supreme authority.

items: Chronological sequence of Dynasties: Slave (1206–1290) → Khalji (1290–1320) → Tughlaq (1320–1414) → Sayyid (1414–1451) → Lodi (1451–1526).
Key Administrative Terms: Iqta (land grant system by Iltutmish), Diwan-i-Arz (military department created by Balban), Diwan-i-Riyasat & Diwan-i-Mustakhraj (Khalji revenue and market departments).
Major Architectural Achievements: Qutub Minar (initiated by Aibak, completed by Iltutmish), Alai Darwaza (Alauddin Khalji), and the city of Agra (founded by Sikandar Lodi in 1504).

blocks.content: Important officials included Wazir, Diwan-i-Arz, Diwan-i-Insha, Diwan-i-Risalat, and Qazi-ul-Quzat.
The empire was divided into Iqtas. Village administration continued with traditional systems.
Agriculture was the backbone of the economy. Land revenue systems like Iqta and Khalisa were followed.
Indo-Islamic architecture developed during this period. Features included arches, domes, minarets, and calligraphy.
This period witnessed interaction between Hindu and Muslim cultures. New social classes emerged.
The Delhi Sultanate declined due to weak rulers, internal conflicts, nobles’ rebellions, and external invasions.

Founder of Delhi Sultanate – Qutbuddin Aibak | Market control – Alauddin Khilji | Token currency – Muhammad bin Tughlaq | First Afghan dynasty – Lodi | End of Sultanate – First Battle of Panipat (1526 AD)
